questions.stem: A 53-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of fevers and worsening skin lesions. The patient had noted progressive development of three distinct purplish nodular lesions on his right arm. He had a history of hypertension, asthma, and HIV . He did not take any regular medications and had no known allergies. The patient lived in Dallas, Texas, with one dog and three cats as pets. He had not had any recent travel overseas and had spent no time in prison or homeless. The patient was sexually active with three partners in the past 6 months. Investigations: CD4 count 25 cells/μL HIV viral load 35,150 copies/mL Syphilis EIA positive Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer 1:2 T. pallidum antibodies (TPHA) positive Lesion biopsy: silver stain showed clumps of darkstaining rods in endothelial cells lining blood vessels
questions.lead_in: What pathogen is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Bartonella henselae The clinical presentation (fevers, purplish nodular skin lesions) in an advanced AIDS patient with characteristic skin biopsy findings is diagnostic for bacillary angiomatosis caused by Bartonella spp. B. henselae is the most common cause in the United States and is typically associated with cat exposure; B. quintana is more commonly seen in Latin America and associated with human body lice and homelessness. The skin biopsy findings would not be consistent with Kaposi sarcoma or syphilis lesions due to Treponema pallidum.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q40

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient presented with fever, weight loss, hepatomegaly, ascites, and papular-nodular skin lesions. He was HIV-positive but had stopped antiretrovirals 3 years previously after poor adherence and intermittent clinic attendance. The lesions had developed from small red papules into large friable nodules, which easily bled on minimal trauma (see image). A skin biopsy was arranged.
questions.lead_in: What stain is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

parts.text: Given his occupation there is high suspicion for Bartonella. What is the recommended treatment for Bartonella endocarditis according to the IDSA?
What other infection would you be considering?

parts_raw.text: Given his occupation, there is a high suspicion for bartonella. What would the recommended treatment for bartonella endocarditis be according to the IDSA?
What other infection would you be considering?

questions.model_answer: a) Confirmed Bartonella endocarditis: doxycycline 100 mg IV/PO q12h for 6 weeks PLUS gentamicin IV for the first 2 weeks; ceftriaxone is added when the diagnosis is only suspected/empiric (culture-negative IE regimen). Surgical valve replacement is required in the majority of cases. b) The other classic cause of blood culture-negative endocarditis in someone with zoonotic/animal exposure is Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) - the most frequently identifiable cause of culture-negative IE in European series, ahead of Bartonella; Brucella is also reasonable given the animal contact.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific endocarditis regimen (doxycycline 6 wk + gentamicin 2 wk, add ceftriaxone if empiric) is from IDSA/Rolain et al. Bartonella treatment guidance; the treatment section is outside this text slice.

cohort_answer.text: CTX/doxy/gent for probable bartonella IE; Gent x 2 weeks/doxy once confirmed IE x 6 weeks. || Coxiella, brucella.

questions.question: A child presents with enlargement of a single cervical lymph node.
questions.question_raw: Child with single cervical LN enlargement.

parts.text: What is the most likely pathogen (to species)?
How do you make the diagnosis?
Outline the optimal management.

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely pathogen (to species)?
How do you make the diagnosis?
Optimal management.

questions.model_answer:
a) Nontuberculous mycobacteria, most commonly Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex (MAC) — now the principal cause of cervicofacial mycobacterial lymphadenitis in otherwise healthy young children, typically a unilateral submandibular/anterior cervical node with indolent progression over 1-3 months.
b) Excisional (complete) node biopsy for histopathology plus acid-fast smear, mycobacterial culture, and species identification (gene sequencing for uncommon species). Excisional biopsy gives the highest microbiologic yield (up to ~90%), and identifying the species is critical because management differs for M. tuberculosis versus NTM.
c) Surgical excision of the involved fluctuant node(s) is the treatment of choice — for both cure and recovery of the organism for susceptibility testing — since NTM are frequently resistant to conventional antituberculous drugs. Adjunctive rifampin plus clarithromycin is considered when complete excision is precluded (e.g., extensive deep involvement, or submandibular nodes abutting the facial nerve).

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: Mycobacterium avium complex. Diagnosis: Biopsy for AFB culture/histopathology. Optimal management: Surgical resection; if abx needed: Clarithromycin, rifampin/ethambutol

questions.question: In culture-negative infective endocarditis, what are the most common causes that would not grow on standard culture media?

parts.text: Culture-negative IE - most common causes that would not grow on standard culture media?

parts_raw.text: Culture negative IE – most common causes that would not grow on standard culture media?

questions.model_answer: Fastidious/intracellular organisms requiring special culture or serology: (1) Coxiella burnetii (Q fever); (2) Bartonella species; (3) Brucella species; (4) Chlamydia species; (5) Legionella species; (6) Tropheryma whipplei; plus fungi (Candida and non-Candida, especially Aspergillus).
questions.beyond_mandell: The consolidated list (Bartonella, Brucella, Legionella, Tropheryma whipplei) is from the AHA/IDSA IE guideline; the chapter slice explicitly covers Coxiella (Duke criteria) and Q fever/Chlamydia therapy.

cohort_answer.text: From IDSA/AHA Guidelines: Bartonella species; Chlamydia species; Coxiella burnetii; Brucella species; Legionella species; Tropheryma whipplei; Candida; non-Candida fungi (particularly Aspergillus species)

parts.text: List/describe the clinical syndromes associated with human bartonellosis.

parts_raw.text: C) List/describe the clinical syndromes assoc with human bartonellosis

questions.model_answer: (1) Cat-scratch disease - regional granulomatous lymphadenitis after cat/kitten contact (B. henselae). (2) Trench fever - self-limited, often quintan (5-day periodic) febrile illness (B. quintana). (3) Oroya fever / verruga peruana (Carrion disease) - biphasic febrile hemolytic illness then eruptive vascular skin lesions (B. bacilliformis). (4) Blood culture-negative endocarditis (B. quintana more than B. henselae). (5) Bacillary angiomatosis / bacillary peliosis in the immunocompromised (advanced HIV, SOT). (6) Ocular/atypical CSD - Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome and neuroretinitis. (7) FUO (children and immunocompromised).

cohort_answer.text: Cat scratch disease; Culture negative IE; Bacillary angiomatosis in HIV+; Trench fever; Carrion's disease/Oroya fever/verruga peruana (Bartonella bacilliformis infection); Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome (granulomatous conjunctivitis in one eye, swollen lymph nodes in front of the ear on the same side)

questions.question: Bartonella henselae infection.

parts.text: Name four clinical scenarios.

parts_raw.text: A) Name 4 clinical scenarios

questions.model_answer: (1) Cat-scratch disease - regional lymphadenopathy with a primary inoculation lesion. (2) Culture-negative endocarditis (typically on a pre-existing abnormal valve/CHD). (3) Ocular disease - Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome or neuroretinitis. (4) Disseminated disease in the immunocompromised - bacillary angiomatosis / bacillary peliosis hepatis, FUO, and hepatosplenic granulomatous lesions.

cohort_answer.text: Cat scratch disease; Culture negative infective endocarditis; Ocular involvement (Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome or neuroretinitis); Cutaneous (primary inoculation lesion, vesicular, erythematous papular); MSK (arthritis/arthralgias, tendonitis, OM); FUO (speaker notes: oculoglandular, endocarditis, adenopathy)

questions.model_answer: a) Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease). b) Azithromycin (500 mg day 1, then 250 mg days 2-5) accelerates lymphadenopathy resolution; the illness is usually self-limited over 1-4 months, and immunocompromised patients may require prolonged therapy.

questions.question: An HIV-positive woman presents with painful bluish lesions on the thigh spreading to the other leg and arm.
questions.question_raw: HIV+ female with painful bluish lesions on thigh and spreading to other leg and arm.

parts.text: What are two organisms that can cause this?

parts_raw.text: What are two organisms that can do this:

questions.model_answer: (1) Bartonella (B. henselae or B. quintana) causing bacillary angiomatosis - vascular, reddish-to-violaceous cutaneous lesions in advanced HIV; (2) Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) causing Kaposi sarcoma, the major clinical differential diagnosis for these lesions in HIV-infected patients.

cohort_answer.text: Bartonella henselae; Bartonella quintana; Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).

questions.question: An HIV-positive patient presents with painful bluish lesions on the thighs spreading to the other leg and arm, with painful lymph nodes in the groin and neck. Biopsy shows vascular proliferation with rod-shaped bacilli on silver stain (Warthin-Starry).
questions.question_raw: HIV+ patient with painful bluish lesions on thighs and spreading to other leg and arm. Painful LN in groin and neck. Bx shows vascular proliferation with rod shaped bacilli on silver stain/warthin starry.

parts.text: Name two organisms that can cause this.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 organisms that can do this?

questions.model_answer: The histology (vascular proliferation with Warthin-Starry-positive bacilli) is diagnostic of bacillary angiomatosis: (1) Bartonella henselae and (2) Bartonella quintana. Either species can produce cutaneous BA lesions in severely immunocompromised (CD4 <100) hosts.

cohort_answer.text: Bacillary angiomatosis caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana. BA characterized by vascular lesions most frequently involving skin, can affect other organs. Rx: erythromycin OR combination of doxycycline 100mg PO/IV q12h plus rifampin 300mg PO bid; optimal duration not known (typically 2-3 months)
